title: De transformatione serierum in fractiones continuas, ubi simul haec theoria non mediocriter amplificatur

deep.reconstruction:
The page continues Theorem III from the previous page. For s = a/α − b/β + c/γ − d/δ + ..., Euler's transformation gives a/s = α + α²b/(aβ − bα + acβ²/(bγ − cβ + bdγ²/(cδ − dγ + ...))). In general the k-th partial numerator is a_{k-1} a_{k+1} α_k² and the k-th denominator is a_{k-1} α_k − a_k α_{k-1}. Re-deriving from the previous page's clearing of fractions gives 'acβ²' for the second numerator, not 'αcβ²'; the examples confirm this.

§30 (continued). The series is s = Σ(−1)^{n+1} n/(n+1) = 1/2 − 2/3 + 3/4 − ..., so a_n = n and α_n = n+1. Euler assigns it the value ln2 − 1/2. This is the Abel/Euler value: the series is 1 − 1 + 1 − ... = 1/2 minus (1/2 − 1/3 + ...) = 1 − ln2. Substitution gives
1/(ln2 − 1/2) = 2 + 1·2·2²/(−1 + 1·3·3²/(−1 + 2·4·4²/(−1 + 3·5·5²/(−1 + ...)))).
The partial numerators are 8, 27, 128, 375, the values of a_{k-1}a_{k+1}α_k² with a_0 = 1. All denominators equal −1.

§31. The series is s = 2/1 − 3/2 + 4/3 − ..., so a_n = n+1 and α_n = n. Its Abel value is 1/2 + ln2. This gives
2/(1/2 + ln2) = 1 + 1·3·1²/(1 + 2·4·2²/(1 + 3·5·3²/(1 + ...))).
The partial numerators are 3, 32, 135, 384, and all denominators are 2·2 − 3·1 = 3·3 − 4·2 = ... = 1. Euler then restates it 'sive' as
4/(2ln2 + 1) = 1 + 1²·3/(1 + 2²·4/(1 + 3²·5/(1 + ...))).

Problem II, §32. Euler treats the power series s = x/α − x²/β + x³/γ − ... and introduces the shifted tails t = x/β − x²/γ + ..., u, v, and so on. Then s = x/α − xt, hence
x/s = α/(1 − αt) = α + α²/(−α + 1/t) = α + α²x/(−αx + x/t).
Iterating with x/t = β + β²x/(−βx + x/u) gives
x/s = α + α²x/(β − αx + β²x/(γ − βx + γ²x/(δ − γx + ...))).
This is the standard Euler continued fraction of a series with reciprocal coefficients. On the next page it is homogenised (x → x/y) and applied to ln(1 + x/y) and to arctan.
errors: In §31 the second form ('sive') is not equivalent to the first. The first CF has partial numerators k(k+2)k² (3, 32, 135, ...), while the 'sive' form has k²(k+2) (3, 16, 45, ...), i.e. a factor k has been dropped. With all partial denominators fixed at 1, no equivalence transformation can change the numerators, and the third convergents already differ (1.0909 vs 1.176). This is either a slip by Euler/editor or a printing error.

Both examples (§30, §31) start from divergent series (terms tend to ±1). Because Euler's transformation makes the convergents equal a/S_n, with S_n the partial sums, the resulting continued fractions oscillate and do not converge. For example, in §30 the convergents are 2, −6, ... corresponding to S_n = 1/2, −1/6, .... The equalities with ln2 − 1/2 and 1/2 + ln2 therefore hold only in a formal/Abel-summation sense, which Euler does not remark on here.
Previous-page Theorem III as transcribed has 'αcβ²' for the second partial numerator; the correct term (and the one used in the examples on this page) is acβ².

ideas.what: Transformation of an alternating series with arbitrary numerators into an equivalent continued fraction whose convergents are the partial sums
ideas.where_published: Introductio in analysin infinitorum I, ch. 18; E593 itself

ideas.what: Applying the CF transformation to divergent series using their Euler/Abel values (ln2 − 1/2, ln2 + 1/2)
ideas.modern_name: formal correspondence of divergent series and continued fractions / summation of divergent series
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (De seriebus divergentibus E247 for the summation viewpoint)
ideas.where_published: E247 and related papers; examples here

ideas.what: Continued fraction for a power series Σ(−1)^{n+1} x^n/α_n via shifted tails: x/s = α + α²x/(β − αx + β²x/(γ − βx + ...))
ideas.modern_name: Euler continued fraction for series with reciprocal coefficients (yields Lambert/Lagrange-type CFs for log and arctan)

deep.surprise_reason: Routine applications of Euler's well-known series-to-continued-fraction transformation. The only notable features are the formal use of divergent series and an apparent slip in the 'sive' restatement in §31.
transcription_corrections: Previous page, Theorem III: second partial numerator should read 'acβ²' (Latin a), not 'αcβ²'; the examples (1.3.3² on this page, 3.4 in §29) confirm this.
Page header '156' and '157': the transcription correctly renders both halves of the two-page spread; the formulas on this page match the image.
